stem: How does Prometheus load alerting and recording rules?

options.text: From YAML rule files listed under rule_files in prometheus.yml
options.note: Right. They reload on SIGHUP.
Alertmanager handles notifications. Rules are evaluated by Prometheus.

options.text: They must be typed into the web UI
options.note: There's no rule editor in the UI. Rules come from files.
Rules aren't defined through labels.

explanation: To include rules in Prometheus, create a YAML file containing the rule statements and load it via the rule_files field in the configuration.
hint: Think about which config key lists them.

stem: How are rules within a rule group evaluated?

options.text: Sequentially, at a regular interval, all with the same evaluation time
options.note: Right. The interval defaults to evaluation_interval.

options.text: In parallel, each with its own random timestamp
options.note: Rules in a group run sequentially with the same evaluation time.

options.text: Only when someone opens the Alerts tab
options.note: Rules are evaluated continuously on a schedule.
They run repeatedly at the group's interval.

explanation: Recording and alerting rules exist in a rule group. Rules within a group are run sequentially at a regular interval, with the same evaluation time. interval defaults to global.evaluation_interval.

stem: Why would you add a recording rule?

options.text: To precompute an expensive or frequently used query, so dashboards query a cheap series
options.note: Right. Especially useful for dashboards that re-run the same query on every refresh.

options.text: To record raw scrape data before relabeling
options.note: That's not what recording rules do.
Notifications come from alerting rules via Alertmanager.
Prometheus doesn't store logs.

explanation: Recording rules precompute frequently needed or expensive expressions and save the result as new series. Querying the precomputed result is often much faster, which is especially useful for dashboards.

stem: What must the record field of a recording rule be?

options.text: A valid metric name, conventionally level:metric:operations
options.note: Right. Its output is stored as series with that name.

options.text: A valid label value, conventionally CamelCase
options.note: That describes alerting rule names.
It's a metric name.
It must be a valid metric name.

explanation: The names of recording rules must be valid metric names. The names of alerting rules must be valid label values.
hint: The result becomes a time series.

stem: With for: 10m on the rule shown, what happens when the expression first returns a series?
code:
- alert: HighRequestLatency
  expr: job:request_latency_seconds:mean5m{job="myjob"} > 0.5
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: High request latency

options.text: The alert becomes pending, and fires only if the condition still holds after 10 minutes of evaluations
options.note: Right. Active but not yet firing means pending.

options.text: The alert fires immediately and stays firing for at least 10 minutes
options.note: That isn't what for does. It delays firing.

options.text: Nothing happens until the next 10-minute boundary
options.note: The alert is pending from the first evaluation.

options.text: Prometheus waits 10 minutes before evaluating the rule again
options.note: Evaluation continues at the group interval.

explanation: The for clause makes Prometheus wait between first seeing a new output element and counting the alert as firing. Elements that are active but not yet firing are pending.
hint: Two states come before an alert is sent.

stem: An alerting rule has no for clause. When does it fire?

options.text: On the first evaluation where the expression returns a result
options.note: Right. The default for is 0s.
There's no 5-minute default. 5 minutes is a recommended value.
for is optional.
It fires on the first evaluation.

explanation: Alerting rules without the for clause become active on the first evaluation. for defaults to 0s.
hint: What's the default value of for?

options.text: Keeps an alert firing for a set time after its condition was last met, to prevent flapping
options.note: Right. Useful for flapping alerts or brief data gaps.

options.text: Delays firing until the condition has held for that long
options.note: That's for, not keep_firing_for.
Repeat intervals are an Alertmanager setting.

options.text: Silences the alert for that long
options.note: Silences are created in Alertmanager.

explanation: keep_firing_for tells Prometheus to keep the alert firing for the specified duration after the firing condition was last met. This can prevent flapping and false resolutions due to missing data.
hint: It acts at the end of an alert's life, not the start.

stem: In an alerting rule, what's the difference between labels and annotations?

options.text: Labels identify and route the alert (such as severity); annotations hold longer descriptive text (summary, description, runbook)
options.note: Right. Both can be templated.

options.text: Annotations are used for routing and labels for descriptions
options.note: Reversed.
They play different roles.

options.text: Labels are only for recording rules
options.note: Alerting rules use labels too, such as severity.

explanation: The labels clause specifies extra labels attached to the alert. The annotations clause specifies informational labels for longer information such as descriptions or runbook links.
hint: Which one would Alertmanager use to decide who gets paged?

stem: Which template inserts the instance label of the alerting series into an annotation?

options.note: Right. $labels holds the alert's label set.
Labels are accessed through $labels.
That isn't Prometheus template syntax.
$value holds the numeric value, not labels.

explanation: The $labels variable holds the alert instance's label key/value pairs, accessed as {{ $labels.<labelname> }}. {{ $value }} holds the evaluated value.
hint: There's a variable holding all labels.

stem: Which synthetic series does Prometheus store for pending and firing alerts?

options.note: Right. Value 1 while in that state.
up is about scrape health.
That's an Alertmanager metric, not the series Prometheus writes for its own rules.

options.text: None. Alerts are only visible in Alertmanager
options.note: Prometheus also stores ALERTS series and shows an Alerts tab.

explanation: For pending and firing alerts, Prometheus stores synthetic series ALERTS{alertname, alertstate, …} with value 1 while the alert is in that state.
hint: The metric name is written in all capitals.

sources.title: Alerting rules › Inspecting alerts during runtime

stem: How can you check a rule file's syntax without starting Prometheus?

options.note: Right. It exits 0 if valid, 1 on errors.
That flag doesn't exist. Use promtool.
amtool checks Alertmanager config, not Prometheus rules.
That reloads a running server. It doesn't check offline.

explanation: Use promtool check rules to check whether a rule file is syntactically correct without starting a Prometheus server. Use promtool test rules for unit tests.

stem: Which component turns firing alerts into email, Slack or PagerDuty notifications?

options.text: Alertmanager, which Prometheus sends alerts to (configured under alerting.alertmanagers)
options.note: Right. Prometheus only evaluates rules and sends alert states.

options.text: Prometheus itself, through a notifications block in the rule
options.note: Prometheus isn't a fully fledged notification solution.
promtool checks and tests rules.
The standard path is Alertmanager.

explanation: Prometheus's alerting rules work out what's broken right now, but they aren't a notification solution. Alertmanager adds summarisation, rate limiting, silencing and routing. Prometheus is configured to send alerts to it.
hint: Prometheus raises alerts; someone else delivers them.
